g.text: SIMULATED DATA
HOW TO USE THIS PACK
Six minutes, then you can argue with it properly
For a PM or delivery lead who has a DoseDay decision to make this week and has never read an interview transcript.
CAPSTONE 02 · GUIDE
3 personas · 1 map · 1 log · 5 interviews
THE ONE THING TO UNDERSTAND IN 30 SECONDS
These three personas are not three slices of your market. They are three failure modes of the same
job — take today’s doses on time — and a feature that fixes one of them will make another one worse.
That trade-off is the reason this pack exists. If you read one line, read that one.
The Shifter
P1 · 59 · “Rowan” · rotating shift work, employer unnamed
FAILS BECAUSE
The app judged them. One missed night became a big red circle,
and they deleted a perfectly good app the next morning.
SO THE PRODUCT
No shame states, ever. Reversible check-in, counted once even
if pressed twice. A “you’re on nights tonight” state instead of
a lecture. Privacy is a choice, not a setting.
GROUNDED 9 · ASSUMPTIONS 2 · 0 stats
One source
Big targets: they read one-handed, glasses off, at the end of a shift.
The Unbothered
P2 · 34 · “Jay” · warehouse team lead · written gender-neutral
FAILS BECAUSE
The app asks for a record, and a record becomes a
judgement: “a dose log makes me a worse person.”
SO THE PRODUCT
One tap and nothing else. No account, no streak, no badge,
no compliance chart, no pep talk. Five seconds is the stated
ceiling on any interaction.
GROUNDED 8 · ASSUMPTIONS 2 · 0 stats
One source
Open question, not a feature: they want no record; P5 wants a full one.
The Unanchored
P3+P4 · 67 and 45 · “Ada” and “Ray” · the one deliberate merge
FAILS BECAUSE
Their routine lives somewhere a routine cannot follow: a
kitchen, a car park, a flight, someone else’s kitchen.
SO THE PRODUCT
The system has to survive a missing routine. One sentence
per medicine. Big targets, dead space to be wrong in, no
tone. Sharing is weekly, chosen, and announced.
GROUNDED 11 · ASSUMPTIONS 2 · 0 stats
Two sources
The weakest thing in the pack: merged on one shared failure, never tested apart.
BEFORE YOU ARGUE WITH A PERSONA: NAMES, PRONOUNS AND TITLES
First names are fictional and exist only so you can remember a person. P3 says “I’m a grown woman” and P4 says
“I’m a grown man”, so those two get gendered pronouns. P1, P2 and P5 never state their own gender, so they are written
neutral — in the cards, on the map, everywhere. And no job title appears for anyone except where a
participant said it themselves: no employer, no industry, no “retired”, no degree. A filename is not evidence.
How to read a persona without fooling yourself
Four rules. The second one is the fastest way to check us.

text.tspan: Quotes are evidence. Adjectives are decoration.

g.text: If a line carries a quote and a participant code, you may build on it. If it does not, it is a hypothesis
and it has to be researched. Every card is split into a grounded count and a named list of assumptions.
Check the trap table. Seven mistakes were planted in the corpus on purpose.
It lives in interviews/00_README_DATA_PROVENANCE.md, and it was withheld — checked against the saved chat, not assumed.
The model caught all seven without it. If a persona statement contradicts that table, the statement is wrong.

text.tspan: Assumption lines are your research backlog, not hedges.

g.text: Each one names a question and a method — a 5-day shift diary, a timed tap test on a low-end device, a travel scenario test — so it can be
scheduled rather than argued about. There are six. None of them is a finding.

text.tspan: Quotations are byte-identical, or they carry an ellipsis.

g.text: If a quote reads too neatly, treat that as a warning. This pack contains four examples of the failure being caught: two in
the model’s draft (V-34, V-35) and two in ours (C-07, C-08). Tidying a quote for line length is how it happens.
How to use the journey map
Five rules for six moments in one day.
Peaks are not where you spend effort. Do not add features at them.
The pill is already taken and attached to a cue that already exists. The job is to stay out of the way.
The troughs are the roadmap. Every priority should trace to one.
Evening dose (−3, P2) and Disrupted days (−4, four participants). Those are the two build targets.
Valence is not effort. A high stage can still be the hardest to design.
P3’s “morning, two of them” is a 4-second tap she still has to find first.
One row is one person. Midday rests on P4 alone — a hypothesis.
The row says so on its face. Do not let a single-source stage quietly become a committed requirement.
No stage is positive except the last. The chart is not drawn to flatter us.
The stage your competitors do not have is Disrupted days. Shift-aware scheduling and a routine that travels live there.
What this pack does not tell you
• Market size, willingness to pay, or clinical outcomes. None of it was measured.
• How a person with no smartphone behaves. No participant represented that case, so
the pack says nothing about it — which is a gap, not a finding.
• Medication correctness. DoseDay records what a clinician entered. No persona is clinical guidance.
• Whether a simulated corpus behaves like real interviews. It does not, by construction.
When real transcripts arrive, regenerate the pack and diff the two verification logs.
Decision checklist for a DoseDay planning session
Ask these six out loud. If any answer is vague, the feature is not ready.
Does it help someone at a trough, or decorate a peak?
Does it require an account, or more than one tap?
Which persona does this make worse? Is that trade named?
Is every claim traceable to a quote, or marked ASSUMPTION?
Is any new copy scolding, or does it imply a judgement?
Does it survive a week when the routine is completely different?

Simulated corpus: no human was interviewed for this pack. Five labelled transcripts, three personas, one critic kept beside them, and a verification log that shows what the AI got wrong and what we got wrong.

A note on the tool: the brief named DeepSeek, which was unreachable from this machine. An authenticated Claude session was used instead, and the substitution is recorded in full, including every model tried and how it failed, in section 0 of the verification log.
